html:
Jane Loevinger conceived ego development as a gradual widening of the frame through which a person interprets experience. Each rung on her "ladder" marks a distinct structure of meaning-making-what the individual can notice, regulate, and integrate about inner life, relationships, and social norms. Movement upward is neither automatic nor universal: most adults consolidate somewhere in the middle, and only sustained reflection plus supportive challenges open the way to the rarer, higher perspectives.

She studied under Erik Erikson in Berkeley

Stages

Pre-Social and Symbiotic (E0-E1). In the newborn and young infant, the ego is only a potential. Experience is a haze of sensation; self and caretaker blur in an undifferentiated symbiosis. Needs are met (or not) without any conscious sense that "I" am separate from "not-me."

Impulsive (E2). With motor mastery and language, the toddler discovers a separable will but lives almost entirely in surging impulses-touch, grab, shout. Rules feel external and arbitrary; guilt is minimal because time, cause and effect, and other minds are not yet coherently represented. The child’s world is vivid but moment-to-moment.

Self-Protective (E3). Fear of punishment and desire for concrete rewards tame raw impulse into strategic compliance. The young school-age child interprets rules instrumentally ("What can I get away with?"), reads others for advantage, and blames circumstances when caught. Morality is pragmatic: loyalty goes to whoever controls the goodies.

Conformist (E4). Around middle childhood the focus shifts from the individual to the tribe. Fitting in, following shared norms, and policing boundaries become paramount. Thoughts are polarized-right or wrong, us or them. Self-esteem rises when peers approve; shame descends when one stands out. Stereotypes and conventional ideals guide judgment. A recent study links ego-development scores to aesthetic construction (Figure) 3. Examples make the construction task and its measurements explicit (Figure).

Self-Aware (E5). The next stage brings a first reflective glimmer: one can compare present norms with alternatives and notice inner feelings distinct from group expectations. Humor and self-criticism appear; contradictions are tolerated if not yet fully resolved. The person can see "how I come across" and entertains multiple points of view, though authority still rests largely outside the self.

"However, the closeness of the self to norms and expectations reveal[s] the transitional nature of these conceptions, midway between the group stereotypes of the Conformist and the appreciation for individual differences at higher levels."

Loevinger considered the Self-Aware (also known as Conscientious-Conformist) stage the "model for adults in our society,"[23] and thought that few passed the stage before at least age twenty-five

She believed that the level produces a "deepened interest in interpersonal relations."

Conscientious (E6). At this stage, norms are internalized and evaluated against personal ideals. Obligations are self-endorsed; guilt becomes an internal moral barometer rather than fear of censure. Long-range goals, nuanced empathy, and the capacity to critique one’s own performance dominate. Life acquires an ethical through-line anchored in responsibility and integrity. Standards are self-chosen, and are distinguished from manners; people are seen in terms of their motives, not just their actions.

Individualistic (E7). The mature adult now recognizes the subjectivity of all frames, including one’s own. Complex emotions-ambivalence, irony, existential doubt-are acknowledged without defensiveness. Relationships permit both intimacy and separateness; tolerance for difference replaces earlier uniformity. Identity is seen as multifaceted and in flux.

According to Loevinger, "To proceed beyond the Conscientious Stage, a person must become more tolerant of himself and of others ... out of the recognition of individual differences and of complexities of circumstances"

A growing concern for psychological causality and development goes hand-in-hand with "greater complexity in conceptions of interpersonal interaction."

Autonomous (E8). Autonomy transcends mere independence: it integrates systems thinking with deep appreciation for others’ autonomy. Conflicts are negotiated through contextual principles rather than fixed rules; growth is prized over stability. The individual manages paradox-freedom and commitment, self and society-without feeling forced to collapse them.

People at this stage are synthesizers, able to conceptually integrate ideas.

The autonomous person "recognizes the limitations to autonomy, that emotional interdependence is inevitable",[34] and may experience a confrontation with the limitations of abilities and roles as part of deepening self-acceptance.

"Self-fulfillment becomes a frequent goal, partly supplanting achievement", and there may be a greater "capacity to acknowledge and to cope with inner conflicts," for example between needs and duties

"A high toleration for ambiguity ... [and] conceptual complexity"[34] (the capacity to embrace polarity, complexity and multiple facets, and to integrate ideas) and "respect for other people’s need for autonomy in clear terms"

Integrated (E9). Reached only by a minority, this stage embodies a fluid, post-autonomous wisdom. Opposites-joy and grief, strength and vulnerability-are embraced as parts of a larger, evolving whole. The self is both grounded and permeable, attuned to the historical and cultural currents in which it moves. Meaning is continually co-created, not merely discovered or imposed

At the integrated stage, "learning is understood as unavoidable ... the unattainable is renounced."

The ego exhibits wisdom, broad empathy towards oneself and others, and a capacity to be aware of inner conflicts (like the individualistic ego) or to tolerate them (like the autonomous ego) and make peace with them

Over the last 25 years Susanne Cook-Greuter and colleagues have argued, on the basis of updated scoring manuals and thousands of protocols, that development can proceed at least two steps further.

The first of these post-autonomous steps has been labelled "Construct-Aware" (also called Ego-Aware, E10). Here, the individual recognizes the very act of meaning-making as a mental construction, sees through language’s tendency to reify experience, and treats the ego itself as an object to be observed rather than defended. Identities, theories and even states of consciousness are held lightly; paradox and impermanence are accepted as givens

A still rarer step, "Unitive" (E11), describes a non-dual stance in which the felt boundary between observer and observed dissolves. People scoring here report a pervasive sense of interconnectedness, effortless compassion and "flow" that is not opposed to ordinary functioning but permeates it. Cook-Greuter finds fewer than one per cent of tested adults in this range.

For Loevinger, climbing the ladder means gaining ever more interior territory to stand on: what was once an unexamined lens (subject) becomes an object one can reflect upon, revise, or transcend. Like Kegan’s orders of consciousness, each transition enlarges the range of perspectives the person can coordinate, making possible richer intimacy, more flexible ethics, and greater resilience in the face of life’s complexity. A 2026 study evaluates automated scoring of ego-development sentence completions (Figure) 1. A complementary study examines self-related trait judgments (Figure) 2.
